QF.id: SIA Assessment Frameworks Techniques and Standards_24

question.text: Which statement BEST describes the rationale for using mixed methods (combining quantitative and qualitative data) in an SIA engagement?

answer.text: Quantitative methods are always superior because numbers don't lie
Qualitative methods are always superior because they capture real stories
Quantitative data provides scale and statistical inference while qualitative data captures context, meaning and mechanisms — together they triangulate causal claims more robustly than either alone
Mixed methods is discouraged under SAS standards because it creates inconsistent reporting

explanation.text: The Logic: Mixed methods combine the strengths of quantitative (scale, statistical inference, SROI monetisation) and qualitative (context, meaning, unexpected outcomes, mechanisms of change). Triangulating both strengthens causal claims and reduces single-method bias. The Trap: Neither method is universally superior — each has blind spots. SAS standards actively encourage triangulation, not discourage mixed methods. Cross-Exam Context: X-A/X-B IA research methodology syllabi teach mixed-methods; XXIII expects the SIA to plan mixed evidence collection under SAS-100 working papers. Assessor's Pro-Tip: Your SIA evidence index should pair every quantitative indicator with at least one qualitative corroboration source (beneficiary interview, FGD note, community-leader statement) — this is the cheapest insurance against a single-source data error.
